>   for(i in 1:N)
>     y_hat[i] <- beta[kk[i]]*(gamma[1]*pred4[i] + gamma[2]*pred5[i] +
>                                        theta[jj[i]] - alpha[kk[i]]);
> }
>
> Also, why not estimate the group-level standard deviations for beta, theta and alpha, rather than setting them at fixed values 4, 1 and 4, respectively, like on page 49 and 50 of the manual?
>

Identifiability.

The IRT problem has a multiplicative and additive invariance that
need to be controlled.  Pinning one of the priors, such as theta,
to a unit normal fixes the scale and location of that parameter.  That
fixes the scale of beta, so you can let alpha have a mean other than 0
or equivalently add an intercept.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Bob that foo(x | theta) feels like an expression that evaluates to something. Namely, I think of normal(x | mu, sigma) as a density function.

But what if the `model` block gets renamed to something suggestive like `posterior contributions` or `probability factors`? Then it would feel like the objects in this block are compounded in the posterior.

factors {
  normal(theta | 0, 1)
  normal(theta | 0, 1)
}

Lionel

2. Other info
(a) I tried to re-create the crash with a simpler model (namely the eyes example from bugs), but the crashes don't occur. So, I am sending the code that crashes.

(c) The crashes occur with all three options for the optimizing algorithm ("LBFGS", "BFGS", and "Newton")

3. Thank you!

Karl Ellefsen

will raise your likelihood to whatever power p you want.

Cheers,

On Tue, Dec 2, 2014 at 8:53 AM, <tom....@uhasselt.be> wrote:

Why do you think that? (that's not a rhetorical question.... do you have some intuition behind this?)

>From what I've seen, it's not the number of intervals that will make Stan run slow. The current ode integrator is not a stiff solver and will break down if the parameter values get into stiff areas.

NUTS / HMC will definitely break down if there are discontinuities in the gradients of the log probability function, which you're doing explicitly. I know that for a fact. It'll still "run" -- just not efficiently.

I would try Bob's suggestion: run the integration in multiple intervals. I think that's the sensible solution at this point. Hopefully we can get this model fit and then we can talk about speed after that.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] case weights in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] case weights in Stan
messages.body_plain:
You just want to multiply the log likelihoods for each data point
directly by the weights and it'll be equivalent to having that many observations,
e.g., with  parameter lambda > 0, observations y[n] >= 0, and weight[n] > 0,

  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(weight[n] * poisson_log(y[n], lambda));

If all weight[n] == 1, this reduces to the usual case.  Usually if you're doing
a  regression instead of lambda, you'd want to use something like:

  poisson_log_log(y[n], beta * x[n]);

which exponentiates the linear predictor (beta * x[n]).

- Bob

On Friday, November 28, 2014 2:37:24 PM UTC-5, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> I prefer having separate files, and use Make or other build tools to build everything. But that's not the only way people use it, especially for quick one-off analyses, so I was just offering some alternatives for those who want everything in a single document.  Especially since knitr and other tools like it are widespread in scientific computing and only growing in usage, I just thought it important to make it as easy as possible to use Stan within them.
>
> With the Stan model in a separate file, the other chunk that's useful to add is one to display the model code:
>
> ```{r results='markup',echo=FALSE,comment=""}
> cat(paste(readLines("foo.stan"), collapse = "\n"))
> ```
>

>
> Another option is to work backwards from an R file with comments using the spin function: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/stitch/
>
> Knitr is a general report generating environment. So can mix chunks of R (or other programming languages) with a variety of markup languages (actually any markup language, since it is customizable). Markdown and LaTeX are the most common, but you can also use knitr with html, reStructuredText, asciidoc and others.  A bunch of examples of knitr using different markup languages are here: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/.  So if you really hate writing markdown, you can use knitr with html: https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/003-minimal.Rhtml.   But, I think that writing it in markdown is the way to go to produce html & pdf.  But the key is good templates, and separating content from presentation. In my workflow, I use make and knitr for Rmd -> md, and then pandoc to convert the markdown file to either or both html and pdf. I don't rely on the default pandoc templates, but write my own.  Rstudio and the package rmarkdown seem to use their own version of templates which seem to be based on pandoc templates since that's what its using in the background  http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/developer_document_templates.html.
>
> In any case, I have an open pull request to add a Stan engine to knitr https://github.com/yihui/knitr/pull/903 ,  so maybe future versions of knitr will include a Stan engine.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

In the data generating process, the observation is kept only iff

w[i]/m[i] < (1-alpha[i])/alpha[i]

(see the R code where I simulate data).

This is a nonlinear constraint on the (w,alpha) space. The easiest way
to express this (for me) was to draw an alpha and a v, and then
transform w from the v.

The Jacobian is triangular, so I think (hope?) that I am doing it
correctly, but if you notice any errors, please tell me.

Thanks for looking at this.

Best,

That's the right solution.

Don't worry about the extra computation done in the generated quantities block. It's done efficiently, without automatic differentiation, and it's done once per iteration. The model block not only executes it, calculated gradients using auto diff, but does this per leapfrog step, which is many times per iteration.

Besides, you can't do it any other way. I'm assuming you're in RStan? You should be able to do it from CmdStan.

Sorry for the slow replies --- we've been hammered with visitors,
travel, and grant writing here at Stan HQ.

I'm not sure why adding the truncation would cause a problem
if all y[n] >= 3.  It might just be slow because we have to
take derivatives of CDFs, which can be hairy.

A few warning messages of the kind you see are OK.  Your negative
binomial shape parameter is wandering off to +infinity.  One
way to fix that is to provide a thinner tailed prior than cauchy(0,1),
but I would've thought that would provide a fair bit of regularization
due to the concentration of mass around 0.

Where do the nb_beta parameters go to?  Truncating those above at 50
is supsicious --- in the non-truncated fit, do the parameters brush
up against those boundaries?  We generally prefer to use soft priors
than hard truncations to avoid issues like parameters running up against
boundaries.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] piecewise (constant) functions in ode's
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] piecewise (constant) functions in ode's
messages.body_plain:
The integrator is already making stops according to the stepsize, but it tries to take large steps when the error tolerances allow it. Integrating in intervals will put a limit on the maximum stepsize and might force much smaller steps than it would otherwise take. Obviously, a piecewise constant function contains discontinuities and the integrator should take small steps around the discontinuity.
However when making long term projections in a multiple dosing regimen, the solution trends to a kind of steady-state and the discontinuities are relatively small. This allows the integrator to still take big steps instead of stopping for the daily dose.

This is just one specific case and does not hold in general. Besides that, there is an overhead in setting up the integrator. I'm not 100% sure how the gradients are computed but this might also give extra costs for multiple integrations. (There was some discussion about adding sensitivities to the ODE system, but from a brief look at the code it seems like reverse-mode autodiff of the integrator)

That said, in the previously attached model I replaced the piecewise constant function with a nice parametrized one. This avoids that problem entirely. Sadly, this "easier" model is also giving troubles indicating additional problems. I've added some print statements to the model (thanks for the tip, didn't know that stan had printing functionality. Much easier than using a debugger) and it seems ok, giving the correct values and log-posterior. But some parameters immediately jump to infinity. I guess the gradient must be incorrect. Is there a way to easily check that, besides the debugger again? :)
The ode integrator breaking down for some parameters will still be an issue in the end because the dynamic system just becomes unstable for some parameters. Finding the correct constraints on the parameters is however no-obvious. But my hope is that if you start somewhere reasonable, there's no need to jump to unstable parameter regions.

Btw: a stiff ode solver might still break down if the system is unstable. I ran into this problem many times and it seems like the sampler should be capable of dealing with these cases if the parameters cannot be constrained somehow.

messages.body_plain:
I'll have to try to get my head around how one of these
stepwise integrators can handle discontinuities.  It might
be more expensive to compute stepwise, though my guess would
be the opposite --- by explicitly telling it where the
discontinuities are, it could then use better stepping between
them.  But I don't have much experience with these algorithms
and none with discontinuous systems.

The integrator has sensitivities added via a nested
reverse mode autodiff.  Our original prototype just
autodiffed the integrator.

You can control the initial jumping into unstable regions
by reducing the initial step size.  You can keep the
jumps small (and thus more curvature respecting) by increasing
the target acceptance rate.  I've found 0.001 and 0.95 to be
pretty stable across ODE cases I've tried so far.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Negative binomial regression for truncated data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Negative binomial regression for truncated data
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for taking time to look at this Bob,

(and apologies for my longish reply)

The derivatives might indeed be the problem. When I run a model without truncation the Gradient evaluation takes 0.06 seconds, and when I run a model with truncation the time taken jumps to 0.45 seconds. These numbers are for a hierarchical regression model with N = 33 000, three groups, and K = 17 predictors.
(with cmdstan--compiled with intel MKL, linux redhat,  2.6 GHz intel processors, 8 or 16GB RAM)

Given the large N and mostly only weakly correlated predictors, the model should not generally be hard to estimate, I assume.

The hard constraint on nb_beta (the beta parameter for the negative binomial) is likely not the problem, because the posterior mean is around 0.9.

I have following ideas to speed up the code, maybe you have an opinion about which is most likely to improve speed (the full model is below)?

(a)
Use more informative priors (i.e. normal(0,1) for betas and chauchy(0,1) for variances.
(I know that nb_beta and all all betas are below 1.) I hope this can address one factor Marc mentioned in his discussion of what influences speed, namely how fast the sampler towards the region of the parameter space with high posteriors.

(b)
Speed up calculations by vectorizing (1) (the second factor Marc mentioned).
In particular, I think of splitting the input by group, i.e. I could submit all relevant variables split by group

Ngrp1, Ngrp2, Ngrp3, ygrp1, ygrp2, ygrp3, xgrp1, xgrp2, xgrp,

which would allow to calculate the means as e.g.

mugrp1 <- beta[1] * xgrp1[1]

instead of looping through all N and do mu[n] <- beta[g[n]] * x[n]

(c)
Speed up by vectorizing (2):
Inspired by Marco (Inacio’s) description of a zero-altered NB regression I thought of doing something along these line:
First increment_log_probs gobally as if there were no truncation:

y ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta)

Then correct for truncation by incrementing again

increment_log_prob(sum(neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta) * is_equalabove_SC))
increment_log_prob(sum(neg_binomial_ccdf_log(SC, alpha,beta) * is_below_SC))

whereby SC is the truncation point and is_equalabove_SC is a vector with zeros for criterion values below the cutoff SC and ones otherwise, so that the sum is calculated only over the relevant rows (the line below is then for below cutoff values).

Somehow I fear that this is a naïve approach, but I think it should be possible to calculate the cdf and ccdf in vectorized form. But this requires that alpha and beta in neg_binomial_ccdf_log(SC, alpha,beta) can be vectors. I didn't try it, but given that the stan reference describes the function as "neg_binomial_cdf(ints n, reals alpha, reals beta)" I hope that the use of plural means that alpha and beta can be vectors.

Lastly, I found that the stan dev branch of includes functions for cdfs and ccdfs for neg_binomilal_2. I have now simply build stan 2.5 after replacing the original neg_binomial_2.hpp with the dev-version. Is this a safe thing to do?

What do you, or anybody else following this discussion, think?

Cheers – Guido

* without going into to many details: In each groups participants over and at/above the truncation/cutoff point are either over or under represented. Think of running a binomial regression to predict number of symptoms in a group that consists to 80% of cases that have more symptoms than the 90th percentile of the population, and 20% of controls that have fewer symptoms.

#################### Model ########################

data {

  int<lower=1> N;     // number of data points
  int<lower=0> y[N];  // observations

  int M;                      // number of groups
  int SC;                    // cut off value for cases (all cases >= cutoff)
  int g[N];                  // group for individual
  int<lower=1> K;     // number predictors (including intercept)
  int<lower=1> L;     // num group predictors

  matrix[N,K] x;        // individual predictors

  matrix[M,L] u;        // group predictors
}

parameters {
  matrix[K,M] z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;               // prior scale
  matrix[L,K] gamma;                      // group coeffs
  real<lower=0.01> nb_beta;          // beta (inv scale) parameter of negative binomial
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[M,K] beta;
  beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
}

model {
  vector[N] mu;         // expected number of symptoms
  tau ~ cauchy(0,1); // orig scale: 2.5
  to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,1); // orig scale: 5

  nb_beta ~ cauchy(0,1);

  for (n in 1:N) {

    mu[n] <- exp(dot_product(x[n],beta[g[n]]));

    if (y[n] < SC)

        y[n] ~ neg_binomial(mu[n]*nb_beta,nb_beta) T[,SC];
    else
        y[n] ~ neg_binomial(mu[n]*nb_beta,nb_beta) T[SC-1,];
  }
}

Xulong:

We’re working on implementing marginal maximum likelihood which ideally will do what you are asking for, it is an approximate inference that in some settings should be much faster. The short answer is that if you use a point estimate for the hyperparameters you will understate uncertainty and also, paradoxically, your estimates can be noisier.  But if runtime is an issue it can make sense to use an approximate method.  It is typically a worse inference from a statistical perspective, but speed can matter.

- chapter 5 of BDA
- this paper:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/chung_etal_Pmetrika2013.pdf
- this paper:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/chung_cov_matrices.pdf
Vince and I also talked about writing a more general paper on this topic but we never got around to writing it.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Negative binomial regression for truncated data
messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 4, 2014, at 5:07 PM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for taking time to look at this Bob,
>
> (and apologies for my longish reply)
>
> The derivatives might indeed be the problem. When I run a model without truncation the Gradient evaluation takes 0.06 seconds, and when I run a model with truncation the time taken jumps to 0.45 seconds. These numbers are for a hierarchical regression model with N = 33 000, three groups, and K = 17 predictors.
> (with cmdstan--compiled with intel MKL, linux redhat,  2.6 GHz intel processors, 8 or 16GB RAM)
>
> Given the large N and mostly only weakly correlated predictors, the model should not generally be hard to estimate, I assume.
>
> The hard constraint on nb_beta (the beta parameter for the negative binomial) is likely not the problem, because the posterior mean is around 0.9.
>
>
>
> I have following ideas to speed up the code, maybe you have an opinion about which is most likely to improve speed (the full model is below)?
>
> (a)
> Use more informative priors (i.e. normal(0,1) for betas and chauchy(0,1) for variances.
> (I know that nb_beta and all all betas are below 1.) I hope this can address one factor Marc mentioned in his discussion of what influences speed, namely how fast the sampler towards the region of the parameter space with high posteriors

This can often help with the number of effective samples per iteration and
also improve the iteration times if you find the iterations in the tails
take longer (they can if you need more leapfrog steps to get a u-turn).

> (b)
> Speed up calculations by vectorizing (1) (the second factor Marc mentioned).
> In particular, I think of splitting the input by group, i.e. I could submit all relevant variables split by group
>
> Ngrp1, Ngrp2, Ngrp3, ygrp1, ygrp2, ygrp3, xgrp1, xgrp2, xgrp,
>
> which would allow to calculate the means as e.g.
>
> mugrp1 <- beta[1] * xgrp1[1]
>
> instead of looping through all N and do mu[n] <- beta[g[n]] * x[n]

This can help with speed.  Anything that lets you call vector-based
log densities with parameters that are mixed vectors and non-vectors
will usually let you reuse computations.

> (c)
> Speed up by vectorizing (2):
> Inspired by Marco (Inacio’s) description of a zero-altered NB regression I thought of doing something along these line:
> First increment_log_probs gobally as if there were no truncation:
>
> y ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta)
>
> Then correct for truncation by incrementing again
>

> increment_log_prob(na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta))
> increment_log_prob(nb*neg_binomial_ccdf_log(SC, alpha,beta))
>
> whereby SC is the truncation point and na  are the number of people with above the truncation point and nb the number of people below.*
>
> Somehow I fear that this is a naïve approach, but I think it should be possible to calculate the cdf and ccdf, or actually the entire experession “na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta)”, only once. But maybe this is already happening under the hood?

This kind of thing can provide a big speedup.  We don't currently reuse
the computation because we don't have a vector-based form of the truncated
densities, which is what we'd need to do it under the hood.

I didn't follow your algebra, but in general, you can do this.  If you
N cases of the same density with truncation below at 2, then you just need

   increment_log_prob(-N * neg_binomial_ccdf(2, alpha, beta));

If the parameters alpha and beta vary by individual, say with a regression,
then this won't work.

There's a discussion in the manual of what's inserted into the log
probability for the various truncations (left/lower, right/upper, both).

- Bob

> > (with cmdstan--compiled with intel MKL, linux redhat,  2.6 GHz intel processors, 8 or 16GB RAM)
> >
> > Given the large N and mostly only weakly correlated predictors, the model should not generally be hard to estimate, I assume.
> >
> > The hard constraint on nb_beta (the beta parameter for the negative binomial) is likely not the problem, because the posterior mean is around 0.9.
> >
> >
> >
> > I have following ideas to speed up the code, maybe you have an opinion about which is most likely to improve speed (the full model is below)?
> >
> > (a)
> > Use more informative priors (i.e. normal(0,1) for betas and chauchy(0,1) for variances.
> > (I know that nb_beta and all all betas are below 1.) I hope this can address one factor Marc mentioned in his discussion of what influences speed, namely how fast the sampler towards the region of the parameter space with high posteriors
>
> This can often help with the number of effective samples per iteration and
> also improve the iteration times if you find the iterations in the tails
> take longer (they can if you need more leapfrog steps to get a u-turn).
>
> > (b)
> > Speed up calculations by vectorizing (1) (the second factor Marc mentioned).
> > In particular, I think of splitting the input by group, i.e. I could submit all relevant variables split by group
> >
> > Ngrp1, Ngrp2, Ngrp3, ygrp1, ygrp2, ygrp3, xgrp1, xgrp2, xgrp,
> >
> > which would allow to calculate the means as e.g.
> >
> > mugrp1 <- beta[1] * xgrp1[1]
> >
> > instead of looping through all N and do mu[n] <- beta[g[n]] * x[n]
>
> This can help with speed.  Anything that lets you call vector-based
> log densities with parameters that are mixed vectors and non-vectors
> will usually let you reuse computations.
>
> > (c)
> > Speed up by vectorizing (2):
> > Inspired by Marco (Inacio’s) description of a zero-altered NB regression I thought of doing something along these line:
> > First increment_log_probs gobally as if there were no truncation:
> >
> > y ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta)
> >
> > Then correct for truncation by incrementing again
> >
> > increment_log_prob(na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta))
> > increment_log_prob(nb*neg_binomial_ccdf_log(SC, alpha,beta))
> >
> > whereby SC is the truncation point and na  are the number of people with above the truncation point and nb the number of people below.*
> >
> > Somehow I fear that this is a naïve approach, but I think it should be possible to calculate the cdf and ccdf, or actually the entire experession “na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta)”, only once. But maybe this is already happening under the hood?
>
> This kind of thing can provide a big speedup.  We don't currently reuse
> the computation because we don't have a vector-based form of the truncated
> densities, which is what we'd need to do it under the hood.
>
> I didn't follow your algebra, but in general, you can do this.  If you
> N cases of the same density with truncation below at 2, then you just need
>
>    increment_log_prob(-N * neg_binomial_ccdf(2, alpha, beta));
>
> If the parameters alpha and beta vary by individual, say with a regression,
> then this won't work.
>
> There's a discussion in the manual of what's inserted into the log
> probability for the various truncations (left/lower, right/upper, both).
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: conceptual question: truncation without closed form
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Suppose I have

- (real) parameters a[N],b[N],m,
- a (known) function f,

and my data generating process is truncated, ie only observations with

f(a[i], b[i]) <= m

are kept in the data. Futhermore, there is no closed form for the
integral

Probability(f(a[i], b[i]) <= m | ...)

so I can't just include it in the likelihood function.

Is there any solution to this in Stan, eg some parameter augmentation or
transformation? Or what is the "standard" way of dealing with these
situations?

As a fallback, I can work out a good approximation to the integral (eg
Pade) and code it in Stan, but if possible I would not mind avoiding
that.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
The last thing that happens in warmup is that the step size
is adapted (the manual has a more detailed description of
adaptation).  This targets an acceptance rate, and if it
can't get the acceptance rate high enough, it will reduce
the step size.

What is the tree depth during sampling (after warmup)?
And the step size?  Do other parameters behave similarly?
Do other chains behave this way or do you have a rough idea of
what the posterior variance is supposed to be?

One possibility is that if you have varying curvature in
the posterior (as in the funnel example in the manual), Stan
can get stuck in the neck (low variance) of the funnel.  This can
happen at any time.  Technically, this is correct behavior to ensure
detailed balance, but it doesn't help you.

- Bob

I'm not sure what you think is an error.  There are a couple compiler
warnings and we're continually trying to silence them, but they're not
a problem.

The warning tagged "Informational message" is informative.
It is indicating that the sampler is running into numerical problems with
the Hamiltonian simulation.  This isn't a concern if it only happens once.
You can reduce the number of such warnings at the cost of speed by reducing
initial step size and increasing the acceptance target, both of which keep
the step size down and reduce discretization (numerical) error in the Hamiltonian
dynamics.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yup --- the compiler warnings can be ignored.

The root cause is that we sometimes code generate variables in the models
through general algorithms that aren't used in particular cases, and those
cause warnings.   For example, we generate a single constant 0 value to avoid
autodiff overhead from repeated use, but it only gets used in models with local
real variables.  Not being used in other cases is not a problem, it just
gives a compiler warning.

- Bob

messages.subject: autodiff for empirical likelihood
messages.subject_clean: autodiff for empirical likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm looking to implement Bayesian inference for empirical likelihood functions.  To make a long story short, the log-likelihood (upon suppressing the data) is of the form loglik(theta) = f( x = theta, y = lambda(theta) ), where theta are the parameters of interest and for given theta, lambda(theta) is the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0.  I don't forsee any difficulties in writing a STAN function, say lambda_calc, which returns the value of lambda(theta).  However, by construction, d/d.theta loglik(theta) is just d/dx f( theta, lambda(theta) ).  I'm wondering whether STAN's autodiff will "know" this or whether I can inform it of this.  I would hate for it to differentiate through the inner workings of lambda_calc...

Thanks,

martin

I have been thinking about things like this for a long time, but it is not implemented yet. Even if you write a while loop to find the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0, Stan won't know the implicit differentiation. Essentially, we need to add the ability to numerically solve general non-linear equations within a Stan program in much the same way we just added the ability to solve ODEs.

Ben

I'm not keen on what Andrew wants, which I believe is something
that has no "data = ..." argument and just looks in the global
environment by default.  Globals are error prone due to the possibility
of accidentally overwriting them (e.g., by downloading some other
package).

But if Ben and Jiqiang think it's OK to do, we could potentially
wait until the model is compiled, then read the variables off
that, then use them as the equivalent of

   data = c("y", "X", "N", ...)

to create the var_context used to read in data.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] suggest a function that can consecutively save posterior samples before all iteration finished
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] suggest a function that can consecutively save posterior samples before all iteration finished
messages.body_plain:
We are going to allow restarts in Stan 3 (no release schedule yet,
but hopefully during early 2015).

Even with the functionality to restart, there is an issue with
warmup.  Until convergence of the warmup estimates (step size and
mass matrix), it's no use running more sampling iterations.  After
warmup has converged, restarting should be no problem.

We're not sure we're going to have exactly reproducible results
from running and saving and restarting --- it will have to round-trip
the double-precision floating-point values through I/O, which we think we
can get right, and also has to save and restart the random number generator
(which will require rewriting our config because restarting is a different
config than seeding with the PRNG we're using).

- Bob

> On Dec 9, 2014, at 10:30 AM, Lee Ang Ling <leean...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> For a large project, it may takes long time to get model converge. If stan can  consecutively save posterior samples before all iteration finished, we can check results early.
>
> for example, the prespecified iteration is 1000, then we can let stan to save result at 200, 400, ...,1000 iteration.
>
> In this way, we may get the desired result without waiting all iteration finished. Or, we can start to compile a new model, if we suspected the model will never converge even all iteration finished.
>
> Is it possible for stan to have this function?
>
> Thanks
>

I might have misunderstood you, but you can use the print statement to see particular values (even calculated values) at every iteration - refer section "24.8 Print Statements" in the Stan 2.5 reference manual p.254.

However, if you print something inside in a loop every iteration it will kill your speed quite dramatically - you might want to refer to the "Print Frequency" section.  I'm afraid I don't know how to access the chain iteration counter - perhaps you can count yourself?

In the past I have used this for some very tedious debugging of a rare event.

Sean

messages.body_plain:
Lee,

If you look at the 8schools model and run it normally it doesn't print anything until the end.  If I add some Stan print statements in the middle of the model then it will print out values to the console as it goes along - it is less than what you want - but it works now.  Refer to the reference manual for more details.  Note again this is Stan syntax not R.  Try running this - it should only take a few seconds since it is small...

8schools-modified.stan
data {
  int<lower=0>J; // number of schools
  real y[J];     // estimated treatment effects
  real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of effect estimates
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  vector[J] eta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[J] theta;
  theta <- mu + tau*eta;
  print("Theta is", theta);
}
model {
  eta ~ normal(0,1);
  y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
  print("y=", y, " and eta=", eta);
}

# the R driver code
library(rstan)
schools_dat <- list(J = 8, y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
                    sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18))
fit <- stan(file = '8schools.stan', data = schools_dat, iter = 100, chains = 1) # smaller run

Kind regards,
Seán

On Tuesday, December 9, 2014 9:07:36 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I have been thinking about things like this for a long time, but it is not implemented yet. Even if you write a while loop to find the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0, Stan won't know the implicit differentiation. Essentially, we need to add the ability to numerically solve general non-linear equations within a Stan program in much the same way we just added the ability to solve ODEs.
>
> Ben
>
> On Tuesday, December 9, 2014 1:44:23 AM UTC-5, mlysy wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I'm looking to implement Bayesian inference for empirical likelihood functions.  To make a long story short, the log-likelihood (upon suppressing the data) is of the form loglik(theta) = f( x = theta, y = lambda(theta) ), where theta are the parameters of interest and for given theta, lambda(theta) is the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0.  I don't forsee any difficulties in writing a STAN function, say lambda_calc, which returns the value of lambda(theta).  However, by construction, d/d.theta loglik(theta) is just d/dx f( theta, lambda(theta) ).  I'm wondering whether STAN's autodiff will "know" this or whether I can inform it of this.  I would hate for it to differentiate through the inner workings of lambda_calc...
> >
> > Thanks,
> >
> > martin

messages.body_plain:
Hi!
I've tried to implement a very simple PK single subject model with one compartment and i.v. bolus dose using the ODE solver integrate_ode.

The model is:
log(V) ~normal(log(muv), sigma2k)
log(k) ~ normal(log(muk), sigma2k)
sigma2e^-1 ~ gamma(a,b)
for (i in 1:ntimes){
z[i] ~ normal(c[i], sigma2e)
}

where c[i]<- q[i]/V  (V is the apparent volume of distribution) and q[i] comes from the resolution of this ODE:

dq/dt=-k*q (k is the rate elimination constant and q represents the amount in the compartment)

The model implemented in stan (one_comp_ode.stan) and the R code (one_comp_ode.R) are in the attachments.

Problems:
 - Why does Stan ask me to set a t0 less than 0?
I try to set t0 less than 0, then I've eliminated the first measure and the first time instance and reset t0 equal to 0 but the algorithm seems to reject always the proposal
(and it is extremely slow).

I would ask if you can tell me where is the problem in my code or if there is another way to do the same thing.
Thanks.

Elisa

How about a function with a short-and-sweet name that you could throw around your data expression, se something like data=f(a,b,z,q), that would pick put the correct things from a given environment.

It could be implemented as:

 f <- function(..., e=.GlobalEnv) { x <- all.names(substitute(list(...))); x <- x[2:length(x)]; o<-lapply(x, get); names(o) <- x; return(o) }
a <- 5
b <- 3
f(a, b, letters)

you should be able to do: stan(..., data=f(a, b))

That way the Stan call would name the required object without having to say from where (global by default) and it would avoid having to name the same thing twice (  list(a=a, b=b)   ).  All we need is a nice short memorable name.  It's even useful if you want to use another environment, but I usually just do:

with(data, stan(.....)) which makes it clear and short.

messages.body_plain:
>
> Am I missing something, or should the SE estimates be the same in both?
>

Hi Bill,

The "sd" column from the output returned by stanlm() is the actual SD of the posterior distribution of the parameters.  The location of the posterior distribution can also vary if you ran the program again with a different seed, starting values, etc., which results in Monte Carlo error on top of the usual sampling error.  The "se_mean" column is an estimate of the Monte Carlo error, but the "sd" is the standard deviation of your posterior, which is analogous to the sampling-error estimate "SE" you see in output from lm() -- and those SEs for intercept and slope also match quite closely to the SDs of the posterior.  I forget what page it is on, but there should be more details in the Stan manual.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: autodiff for empirical likelihood
messages.subject_clean: autodiff for empirical likelihood
messages.body_plain:
I don't think there is any way to do it with just Stan code, but it is pretty straightforward (in a particular case) if you write the C++ code.

There is this for implementing new functions in general:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

In this particular case, you need a function that
Solves for the root of the implicit function with regular double variables. There are many tools in Boost for this.
Returns the solution in special Stan var variables that takes into account the implicit differentiation, i.e. the sensitivities of the solution to the parameters declared in the parameters block. There are many examples of doing this in the Stan library (e.g. softmax.hpp). Technically, you should get it to work with both forward mode and reverse mode autodiff and there are subdirectories under $STAN_HOME/src/stan/agrad for each.

Ben

> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/EDu4GLsc5Ik/E2E2o7tqOuAJ
>
> Are you aware of any more detailed step-by-step instructions to do this?

> On Tuesday, December 9, 2014 9:07:36 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > I have been thinking about things like this for a long time, but it is not implemented yet. Even if you write a while loop to find the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0, Stan won't know the implicit differentiation. Essentially, we need to add the ability to numerically solve general non-linear equations within a Stan program in much the same way we just added the ability to solve ODEs.
> >
> > Ben
> >
> > On Tuesday, December 9, 2014 1:44:23 AM UTC-5, mlysy wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > I'm looking to implement Bayesian inference for empirical likelihood functions.  To make a long story short, the log-likelihood (upon suppressing the data) is of the form loglik(theta) = f( x = theta, y = lambda(theta) ), where theta are the parameters of interest and for given theta, lambda(theta) is the solution to d/dy f(theta, lambda) = 0.  I don't forsee any difficulties in writing a STAN function, say lambda_calc, which returns the value of lambda(theta).  However, by construction, d/d.theta loglik(theta) is just d/dx f( theta, lambda(theta) ).  I'm wondering whether STAN's autodiff will "know" this or whether I can inform it of this.  I would hate for it to differentiate through the inner workings of lambda_calc...
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > >
> > > martin

messages.body_plain:
We should make this clearer in the manual, because
you're not the only one who's raised this question.

  * t0 is the initial time
  * y0 is the initial state
  * ts is the array of requested solution times

There is a requirement that ts[i] > 0 (strictly) for all i.

If there's measurement error on the initial state y0,
you need to make y0 a parameter and then model the measurement
error directly.

Otherwise, the model looks OK to me --- you have all the necessary
constraints on parameters.  You could make sigmae
and/or theta local variables in the model, unless you want to save
sigmae in addition to taue.  I don't see any reason to save theta since
it's just an array containing k.

- Bob

Hey Guys,

Still very new to Stan/programming/statistics in general, so I'm building my mental map in regards to how everything works.

I am trying to fit the results of an output of diffeqs solved via the Euler method to two vectors of data, which I will call u1array and u2array.

A simplified pseudocode of the model, where c1 and c2 are parameters.:

I = linspace(0,1,11)
dt = 0.1
ttotal = 1000
eulersteps = int(ttotal/dt)
u1hatarray = []
u2hatarray = []
for I1 in I
    for I2 in I
        for i in 1:eulersteps
            V1 += dt * (c1 * I1 + c2 * I2)
            V2 += dt * (c1 * I2 + c2 * I1)
        u1hatarray.append(V1)
        u2hatarray.append(V2)

Now, would it be possible to fit u1hatarray and u2hatarray to u1array and u2array? All the examples I've come across so far have depicted fitting single data vectors?

messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can do what you want in Stan, but you'll have
to code it in Stan's syntax.

For multivariate normal, you ideally want to parameterize
in terms of Cholesky factors and use multi_normal_cholesky
or for 2D, just build the covariance matrix out of two scales
and a correlation.

There are lots of examples in the regression chapter of the manual.
And in the ODE chapter --- we have a built-in ODE solver.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The main problem is that you can't fit hierarchical models with
optimization unless you are very careful with priors (see Gelman et al.'s
papers on this topic).

The second problem is that we only compute the log density up to a constant
normalizing term, and it includes the prior as well as the likelihood,
so you can't directly compare log likelihoods this way.  You could compute
the log likelihood in your model if you want, say in generated quantities.
If you use the functional forms (e.g. normal_log(y,mu,sigma) instead of
the sampling notation form y ~ normal(mu,sigma)), we include all the normalizing
terms.

- Bob

By your analogy, you would also want

x <- rnorm(100)
mean()

to work because the first argument to the mean function is x and an object called x exists in the global environment. Your preferred behavior relies on the fact that the declared names of the variables in the data block of the Stan program are the same as their symbol names in R and that you are calling stan() from the global environment instead of calling stan() from another function. Subtle errors and undefined behavior can crop up otherwise.

R only behaves the way you want when you utilize an environment, as in

lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dataset)
with(dataset, lm(y ~ x1 + x2))
do.call(lm, args = list(formula = y ~ x1 + x2), envir = .GlobalEnv)

Similarly, Stan would behave the way you want it to if you just called

stan(file, data = .GlobalEnv)
stan(file, data = dataset)

except that you if the data argument includes any objects that Stan cannot handle, then an error is thrown currently. We could possibly not throw that error if the object does not correspond to any variable declared in the data block of a Stan program.

messages.body_plain:
If we do this (which I'll go on record as objecting to because of
its lack of transparency and its dependence on globals), then we
shouldn't leave it the way it is now where it will pull everything
out of the blog environment into a var_context --- it's going to
make all the behavior depend not only on the relevant global vars,
but also irrelevant ones.

Let's try to at least remain as modular as possible.

So what I'd propose (if we do this) is to add a new code-generated
method to the generated model class

   std::vector<std::string> data_variable_names();

that returns a vector of data variable names.  This should only take
me a day or so, including testing.

Then, we would create a var_context from the model and an environment
(defaulting to the global environment) that would pull out all the
variables named in the model from the global environment to create
a var_context.

My main objection to all of this is that it's not clear from the call
stan(...) which dependencies there are on the global environment.  You
need to look inside the file/string defining the Stan model for that.

I can also anticipate Andrew's next request, which will be to pull out of the
list just the variables given by the list, and pull the rest out of the
global environment, but maybe we should punt on that (though the
stacking/chainging/whatevering var_context should allow it pretty easily).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Even if I translate the time vector of a certain constant, i.e. t=t+10, Stan requires me to set a t0 minor then 10. So, is it right that t0 can't be fixed at the first element of the time vector?
As regarding the initial condition y0, in my case I want to fix the amount in the compartment equal to the dose amount to simulate a bolus injection. Neverthless when I run the script, the algorithm seems not to move from the first iteration also after a long time.
This is the message that appears:

Iteration:    1 / 10000 [  0%]  (Warmup)

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#INF:0, but must be finite!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I've attached the scripts with the changes I've made.

2014-12-10 20:26 GMT+01:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:

> We should make this clearer in the manual, because
> you're not the only one who's raised this question.
>
>   * t0 is the initial time
>   * y0 is the initial state
>   * ts is the array of requested solution times
>
> There is a requirement that ts[i] > 0 (strictly) for all i.
>
> If there's measurement error on the initial state y0,
> you need to make y0 a parameter and then model the measurement
> error directly.
>
> Otherwise, the model looks OK to me --- you have all the necessary
> constraints on parameters.  You could make sigmae
> and/or theta local variables in the model, unless you want to save
> sigmae in addition to taue.  I don't see any reason to save theta since
> it's just an array containing k.
>
> - Bob

>
> > On Dec 10, 2014, at 5:57 AM, eli...@universitadipavia.it wrote:
> >
> > Hi!
> > I've tried to implement a very simple PK single subject model with one compartment and i.v. bolus dose using the ODE solver integrate_ode.
> >
> > The model is:
> > log(V) ~normal(log(muv), sigma2k)
> > log(k) ~ normal(log(muk), sigma2k)
> > sigma2e^-1 ~ gamma(a,b)
> > z[i] ~ normal(c[i], sigma2e)
> >
> > c[i] comes from this ODE:
> >
> > dq(t)/dt=-k*q/t) (k is the rate elimination constant and q represents the amount in the compartment)
> >
> > c(t)=q(t)/V (V is the apparent volume of distribution)
> >
> > The model implemented in stan (one_comp_ode.stan) and the R code (one_comp_ode.R) are in the attachments.
> >
> > Problems:
> >  - Why does Stan ask me to set a t0 less than 0?
> > I try to set t0 less than 0, then I've eliminated the first measure and the first time instance and reset t0 equal to 0 but the algorithm seems to reject always the proposal
> > (and it is extremely slow).
> >

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 11, 2014, at 4:21 AM, Elisa Borella <elisa.b...@universitadipavia.it> wrote:
>
> Even if I translate the time vector of a certain constant, i.e. t=t+10, Stan requires me to set a t0 minor then 10. So, is it right that t0 can't be fixed at the first element of the time vector?

Correct.  All elements of the time vector must be strictly
greater than t0.

> As regarding the initial condition y0, in my case I want to fix the amount in the compartment equal to the dose amount to simulate a bolus injection.

That's what we've done, as well.

That means that y0 is the value for t0.  There's nothing
to solve, which is why it's not in the list of times.

> Neverthless when I run the script, the algorithm seems not to move from the first iteration also after a long time.
> This is the message that appears:
>
> Iteration:    1 / 10000 [  0%]  (Warmup)
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#INF:0, but must be finite!
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

This message is saying that you have a normal(...) somewhere that
is getting an infinite mean.  Sorry we don't have line-by-line
error messages yet --- it's on our to-do list.

It's hard to say more without seeing the model.  You might want to
try running in diagnostic mode just to make sure your init is
well formed.

Then, try running with a small initial step size, like 0.001 to see
if that helps you move.   It controls the discretization of the
Hamiltonian simulation (itself solving an ODE within an iteration),
and making it smaller lets it follow the curvature of the posterior
more closely.

A problem that can arise is that the parameters will wander into
values that cause the ODE to become stiff.  Stan's going to grind to
a halt when that happens, at least until we add a stiff solver, which
is one of our highest priorities at the moment and should happen in
the next six to nine months if not sooner.  The smaller initial step
size can help (as can a higher target acceptance rate for adaptation,
which will keep the step size smaller).

Also, the more informative you can make the priors, the better --- it
will help prevent the parameters from wandering into stiff territory.

- Bob

more experience ourselves with the current setup.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initial time in ode_integrate?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Initial time in ode_integrate?
messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 11, 2014, at 2:03 PM, Elisa Borella <elisa.b...@universitadipavia.it> wrote:
>
> 1. It's hard to say more without seeing the model. -> The model is described in the first mail where I provided also the .stan and .R codes.

Thanks.  I forgot you'd posted it already.

I think the problem is in your definition of the ODE system.

Your code is this:

   dydt[1] <- -theta[1] * y[1];

But your math is this:

> dq(t)/dt=-k*q/t) (k is the rate elimination constant and q represents the amount in the compartment)

So it looks like you're missing the division by t in the system definition.

> 2.the more informative you can make the priors -> Setting the priors more strictly (not only the lower bound at 0 but also the upper bound), the algorithm runs, but despite this the parameters estimated are different from those used to simulate the data (so the real parameters). I implemented the model also in another software for Bayesian analysis (using always a ODE solver) and in that case the parameters are estimated correctly. Couldn't be the integrate_ode function the responsible for this? If I don't use the ODE, but the analytical solution (c(t)=D/V * exp(-k*T) ) the parameters are estimated correctly!

My guess is that it's in the coding of the ODE system, not in
the ODE solver.

As we discussed earlier, you also shouldn't have t = 0 in your
array of solution times if t0=0 is your initial time.  If you
want to model noise in the initial state, you need a separate
statement in Stan.

> Here is a comparison between the estimated parameters in both the cases and the real ones:
>

...

> 3. try running with a small initial step size -> If I would set the integration step where should I put the value? In an argument of the integrate_ode function? Which one? (I didn't found nothing about this on the manuals)

I meant the initial step size for the Hamiltonian integrator we use
for sampling on the outside, not for the ode_integrate() function on the
inside.  The step size determines how long the discretization interval
is for the Hamiltonian simulation over the parameters.  How to set it
depends on whether you're using RStan, PyStan, CmdStan, etc.  In RStan, it's
another argument to stan() or sampling():

  control = list(stepsize=0.001)

You may also find it helpful to up the adaptation acceptance target to keep
the step size low at convergence, maybe something like:

  control = list(stepsize=0.001, adapt_delta=0.95)

This is all independent of the step size in the Runge-Kutta integrator used
for integrate_ode().  That one can't be controlled yet, but we'll make it
configurable in the future.

- Bob

- Bob, before elaborating the details, I want to gladly report that the model is working, if not too early to say so. Here are what I did:

1. Declared primitive cut points as simplex, put dirichlet prior on them, declared ordered positive cut points from cumsum of the primitive cut points with a chosen scale factor (I used 10), also put the first cut point as 0. I think this should resolve the scalability issue.

2. Add an intercept parameter in the ordered categorical model with cauchy(0, 0.5) prior, given the fact that I fixed the first cut point at 0. Together with the last step, this should resolve the identificability issue.

3. Constrain the deviation parameter more, that is the sigmaU in the model. You pointed this out in your previous post, and I found out from my diagnosis sigmaU is really the key. When estimations go insane, the sigmaU values always went crazy, can be more than 100. Now, I constrained sigmaU lower as 0.001, upper as 1, and a little more stringent prior as half cauchy(0, 0.5). I believe the current constrain is reasonable if you also agree. I understand we can not put too much constrain on sigmaU, otherwise we will underestimate the random effect. I also have the multivariate normal primitive parameter z in the model that follows normal(0, 1), which is pretty broad. It is sigmaU * (CK * z) together that define the random effect. So I think the whole strategy should be fine theoretically.

4. Put user-defined initial values instead of the random. I put the optimizing() output from one marker as initial values of all other markers. This significantly decrease the estimating time.

I want to report the above strategies also resolve the problem as reported in another post of mine: Ordered categorical model with known covariance matrix not converging. It was the same model, same data, instead implemented by sampling. MCMC converged well, and results are similar with that of the optimizing method. When tested on simulated data, the peak was clear and correctly positioned in the WAIC plot.

Please let me know if you see anything problematic, and any other things I should do to check the sanity.

Best,

Xulong

I believe the current constrain is reasonable if you also agree. I understand we can not put too much constrain on sigmaU, otherwise we will underestimate the random effect. I also have the multivariate normal primitive parameter z in the model that follows normal(0, 1), which is pretty broad. It is sigmaU * (CK * z) together that define the random effect. So I think the whole strategy should be fine theoretically.
>
> 4. Put user-defined initial values instead of the random. I put the optimizing() output from one marker as initial values of all other markers. This significantly decrease the estimating time.
>
> I want to report the above strategies also resolve the problem as reported in another post of mine: Ordered categorical model with known covariance matrix not converging. It was the same model, same data, instead implemented by sampling. MCMC converged well, and results are similar with that of the optimizing method. When tested on simulated data, the peak was clear and correctly positioned in the WAIC plot.
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Negative binomial regression for truncated data
messages.body_plain:
If you know phi should be around 10, then this is probably
not the right prior:

  phi ~ cauchy(0,1);

You should be able to use something that doesn't put a hard
bound on phi (the negative binomial overdispersion).

You could make beta local variable in model and avoid writing the output.

I think the combination of this

>  eta_b[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]));

and this

>   increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(y_b,eta_b,phi));

may be a mistake, because it amounts to:

  y_b ~ neg_binomial_2(y_b, exp(eta_b), phi);

which is equivalent to:

  y_b ~ neg_binomial_2(y_b, exp(exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]))), phi);

Our doc for negative binomial 2 should really be broken out to indicate
that neg_binomial_2_log is yet another parameterization.

You could simplify this a bit

> for (n in 1:N_b){
>     eta_b[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]));
>     psi_b[n] <- dot_product(x_b[n],alpha);}
>
>   // increment zero alteration
>   z_a ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_a);
>   z_b ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_b);

by just writing this:

  z_b ~ bernoulli_logit(x_b * alpha);

If you really want the loop, it's better to use an array of vectors
than a matrix if you're pulling out rows because there's no copying.

- Bob

> On Dec 15, 2014, at 3:39 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I am posting the best I could come up with to vector as much as possible.
>
> A brief reminder of what I am trying to model:
> - I want to fit a hierarchical (zero altered) negative binomial regression model
> - The groups I model consist of 2 groups with many individuals above a threshold and few individuals below a threshold, as well as a third group with the opposite distribution (see attached figure)
> - To model these "funny" outcome distribution, I split outcomes (y) into those smaller than the threshold (y_a) and those equal to or larger than the threshold (y_b) and then model y_a and y_b with truncated distributions.
>
> The complete model is below.
> When I ran this model with on my full data set (N = 30000 for group 1 and 1500 for groups 2 and 3, respectively), it took around 88 hours to complete 375 iterations (i.e. around 15 minutes per iteration). A Gradient evaluation takes 0.56s.
> So before I actually start such an analysis, it would be great if anybody could have a look at the model below and suggest improvements.
>
> Best Guido
>
> ################## MODEL ############################
> // Hierachical Zero altered negative binomial regression model for truncated data
> data {
>   // to allow better vectorization
>   // data is split into .._a for right-truncated
>   // and .._b for left_truncated outcomes
>   int<lower=1> N_a;         // number of data points
>   int<lower=0> y_a[N_a];    // observations
>   int<lower=0> z_a[N_a];    // indicator: observation is not zero
>   int g_a[N_a];             // group for individual
>   int<lower=1> N_b;         // number of data points
>   int<lower=0> y_b[N_b];    // observations
>   int<lower=0> z_b[N_b];    // indicator: observation is not zero
>   int g_b[N_b];             // group for individual
>   int SC;    // truncation / cut off point
>   int<lower=1> K;           // number parameters
>   int<lower=1> L;           // number group predictors
>   matrix[N_a,K] x_a;        // individual predictors
>   matrix[N_b,K] x_b;        // individual predictors
>   int M;                    // number of groups
>   matrix[M,L] u;            // group predictors
> }
>
> parameters {
>   // covariances for regression model parameters for mean of negative binomial
>   // (from stan language reference)
>   matrix[K,M] z;
>   cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] tau;           // prior scale
>   matrix[L,K] gamma;                // group coeffs
>
>   // parameters for regression model for p(score = 0) (zero alteration)
>   // no hierarchical estimation here because some groups have only a few zeros
>   vector[K] alpha;                // group coeffs
>
>   // variance of negative binomial
>   // I know from previous analysis that it should be around 10
>   real<lower=0,upper=15> phi;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   // regression weights for mean of negative binomial model
>   matrix[M,K] beta;
>   beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
> }
>
>
> model {
>   // mean on negative binomial
>   vector[N_a] eta_a;
>   vector[N_b] eta_b;
>   // zero alteration
>   vector[N_a] psi_a;
>   vector[N_b] psi_b;
>
>   / sample parameters
>   tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); # orig scale = 2.5
>   to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
>   L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
>   to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,5); # orig scale = 5
>   phi ~ cauchy(0,1);
>   alpha ~ normal(0,5); # orig scale = 5
>
>
>   // prepare and partially update for y_a < SC
>   for (n in 1:N_a){
>     eta_a[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_a[n],beta[g_a[n]]));
>     psi_a[n] <- dot_product(x_a[n],alpha);
>     // because this is a zero altered negative binomial
>     // and y_a < SC, I model y_a as being truncated
>     // at the right- and left-hand side
>     increment_log_prob(-log_diff_exp(neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(SC-1,exp(eta_a[n]),phi),
>                                      neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(0,exp(eta_a[n]),phi)));}
>
>   // prepare for y_b >= SC
>   for (n in 1:N_b){
>     eta_b[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]));
>     psi_b[n] <- dot_product(x_b[n],alpha);}
>
>   // increment zero alteration
>   z_a ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_a);
>   z_b ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_b);
>
>   // increment negative binomial model
>   increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(y_a,eta_a,phi));
>   increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(y_b,eta_b,phi));
>
>   // increment for left hand side truncation of y_b
>   increment_log_prob(-neg_binomial_2_ccdf_log(SC-1, exp(eta_b),phi));
> }
>
>

> > (I know that nb_beta and all all betas are below 1.) I hope this can address one factor Marc mentioned in his discussion of what influences speed, namely how fast the sampler towards the region of the parameter space with high posteriors
>

> take longer (they can if you need more leapfrog steps to get a u-turn).

> > (b)

> > In particular, I think of splitting the input by group, i.e. I could submit all relevant variables split by group
> >
> > Ngrp1, Ngrp2, Ngrp3, ygrp1, ygrp2, ygrp3, xgrp1, xgrp2, xgrp,

> > which would allow to calculate the means as e.g.
> >
> > mugrp1 <- beta[1] * xgrp1[1]
> >
> > instead of looping through all N and do mu[n] <- beta[g[n]] * x[n]
>
> This can help with speed.  Anything that lets you call vector-based
> log densities with parameters that are mixed vectors and non-vectors
> will usually let you reuse computations.
>
> > (c)
> > Speed up by vectorizing (2):
> > Inspired by Marco (Inacio’s) description of a zero-altered NB regression I thought of doing something along these line:
> > First increment_log_probs gobally as if there were no truncation:
> >
> > y ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta)
> >
> > Then correct for truncation by incrementing again
> >
> > increment_log_prob(na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta))
> > increment_log_prob(nb*neg_binomial_ccdf_log(SC, alpha,beta))
> >
> > whereby SC is the truncation point and na  are the number of people with above the truncation point and nb the number of people below.*
> >
> > Somehow I fear that this is a naïve approach, but I think it should be possible to calculate the cdf and ccdf, or actually the entire experession “na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta)”, only once. But maybe this is already happening under the hood?
>
> This kind of thing can provide a big speedup.  We don't currently reuse
> the computation because we don't have a vector-based form of the truncated
> densities, which is what we'd need to do it under the hood.
>
> I didn't follow your algebra, but in general, you can do this.  If you
> N cases of the same density with truncation below at 2, then you just need
>
>    increment_log_prob(-N * neg_binomial_ccdf(2, alpha, beta));
>
> If the parameters alpha and beta vary by individual, say with a regression,
> then this won't work.
>
> There's a discussion in the manual of what's inserted into the log
> probability for the various truncations (left/lower, right/upper, both).
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Update on Stan.jl (Stan for Julia users)
messages.subject_clean: Update on Stan.jl (Stan for Julia users)
messages.body_plain:
Stan’s home page contains a link to a Julia interface to Stan.jl for those interested in Stan + Julia.

Below a short update on what has changed over the last 2 months or so:

1. Fixed several issues to make Stan.jl work on Windows.

2. Using Mamba to display and diagnose simulation results.

    The call to stan() to sample now returns a Mamba Chains object (previously it returned a dictionary).

3. The ability to select which variables to extract form Stan’s output .csv file(s).

    Saves time if there are many, many observed variables.

4. Inline definition of model and data in the .jl file.

    Compile only the first time or when the model is modified (as detected by ‘make’). Or use an external .stan file.

5. The ability to execute Stan simulations in parallel.

    This is in fact the default.

6. JuliaBox

    For those who don’t want to install *any* software, have an account on JuliaBox and access to a browser.

    Thanks to Viral, Tanmay and Shashi for installing CmdStan on JuliaBox! JuliaBox gives users a Notebook like interface.

    A few example notebooks are included in Stan.jl v”0.2.0” in the Examples/Notebooks subdirectory.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@mac.com

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Negative binomial regression for truncated data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Negative binomial regression for truncated data
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the pointers Bob!

I think the doc for neg_binomial_2 is ok. The root of my error was that the eta-parameterization is available for neg_binomial_2_log in the form of neg_binomial_2_log_log, but there is no such thing as
neg_binomial_2_cdf_log_log, so that I went back and forth about where to do the exponentiation and in the end screwed it up.
maybe a more intuitive naming scheme would be neg_binomial_.. (for the alpha, beta parameterization) , neg_binomial_mu_... (for the mu, phi parameterization) and neg_binomial_eta_... (for the eta, phi parameterization)?

When going through the code again it appeared to me that I incorrectly also incremented the log-probability for zero values in y_a and y_b with the likelihood from the negative_binomial.
I fixed this in the updated model by including an additional outcome-vector y0, which is zero or 1 for non-zero outcomes.

The updated model (attached) is still slow, but I know believe that this is mostly due to the large amount of data.

Cheers - Guido

On Monday, December 15, 2014 7:10:19 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If you know phi should be around 10, then this is probably
> not the right prior:
>
>   phi ~ cauchy(0,1);
>
> You should be able to use something that doesn't put a hard
> bound on phi (the negative binomial overdispersion).
>
> You could make beta local variable in model and avoid writing the output.
>
> I think the combination of this
>
> >  eta_b[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]));
>
> and this
>
> >   increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(y_b,eta_b,phi));
>
> may be a mistake, because it amounts to:
>
>   y_b ~ neg_binomial_2(y_b, exp(eta_b), phi);
>
> which is equivalent to:
>
>   y_b ~ neg_binomial_2(y_b, exp(exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]))), phi);
>
> Our doc for negative binomial 2 should really be broken out to indicate
> that neg_binomial_2_log is yet another parameterization.
>
> You could simplify this a bit
>
> > for (n in 1:N_b){
> >     eta_b[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]));
> >     psi_b[n] <- dot_product(x_b[n],alpha);}
> >
> >   // increment zero alteration
> >   z_a ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_a);
> >   z_b ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_b);
>
> by just writing this:
>
>   z_b ~ bernoulli_logit(x_b * alpha);
>
> If you really want the loop, it's better to use an array of vectors
> than a matrix if you're pulling out rows because there's no copying.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Dec 15, 2014, at 3:39 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am posting the best I could come up with to vector as much as possible.
> >
> > A brief reminder of what I am trying to model:
> > - I want to fit a hierarchical (zero altered) negative binomial regression model
> > - The groups I model consist of 2 groups with many individuals above a threshold and few individuals below a threshold, as well as a third group with the opposite distribution (see attached figure)
> > - To model these "funny" outcome distribution, I split outcomes (y) into those smaller than the threshold (y_a) and those equal to or larger than the threshold (y_b) and then model y_a and y_b with truncated distributions.
> >
> > The complete model is below.
> > When I ran this model with on my full data set (N = 30000 for group 1 and 1500 for groups 2 and 3, respectively), it took around 88 hours to complete 375 iterations (i.e. around 15 minutes per iteration). A Gradient evaluation takes 0.56s.
> > So before I actually start such an analysis, it would be great if anybody could have a look at the model below and suggest improvements.
> >
> > Best Guido
> >
> > ################## MODEL ############################
> > // Hierachical Zero altered negative binomial regression model for truncated data
> > data {
> >   // to allow better vectorization
> >   // data is split into .._a for right-truncated
> >   // and .._b for left_truncated outcomes
> >   int<lower=1> N_a;         // number of data points
> >   int<lower=0> y_a[N_a];    // observations
> >   int<lower=0> z_a[N_a];    // indicator: observation is not zero
> >   int g_a[N_a];             // group for individual
> >   int<lower=1> N_b;         // number of data points
> >   int<lower=0> y_b[N_b];    // observations
> >   int<lower=0> z_b[N_b];    // indicator: observation is not zero
> >   int g_b[N_b];             // group for individual
> >   int SC;    // truncation / cut off point
> >   int<lower=1> K;           // number parameters
> >   int<lower=1> L;           // number group predictors
> >   matrix[N_a,K] x_a;        // individual predictors
> >   matrix[N_b,K] x_b;        // individual predictors
> >   int M;                    // number of groups
> >   matrix[M,L] u;            // group predictors
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >   // covariances for regression model parameters for mean of negative binomial
> >   // (from stan language reference)
> >   matrix[K,M] z;
> >   cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
> >   vector<lower=0>[K] tau;           // prior scale
> >   matrix[L,K] gamma;                // group coeffs
> >
> >   // parameters for regression model for p(score = 0) (zero alteration)
> >   // no hierarchical estimation here because some groups have only a few zeros
> >   vector[K] alpha;                // group coeffs
> >
> >   // variance of negative binomial
> >   // I know from previous analysis that it should be around 10
> >   real<lower=0,upper=15> phi;
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >   // regression weights for mean of negative binomial model
> >   matrix[M,K] beta;
> >   beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
> > }
> >
> >
> > model {
> >   // mean on negative binomial
> >   vector[N_a] eta_a;
> >   vector[N_b] eta_b;
> >   // zero alteration
> >   vector[N_a] psi_a;
> >   vector[N_b] psi_b;
> >
> >   / sample parameters
> >   tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); # orig scale = 2.5
> >   to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
> >   L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
> >   to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,5); # orig scale = 5
> >   phi ~ cauchy(0,1);
> >   alpha ~ normal(0,5); # orig scale = 5
> >
> >
> >   // prepare and partially update for y_a < SC
> >   for (n in 1:N_a){
> >     eta_a[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_a[n],beta[g_a[n]]));
> >     psi_a[n] <- dot_product(x_a[n],alpha);
> >     // because this is a zero altered negative binomial
> >     // and y_a < SC, I model y_a as being truncated
> >     // at the right- and left-hand side
> >     increment_log_prob(-log_diff_exp(neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(SC-1,exp(eta_a[n]),phi),
> >                                      neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(0,exp(eta_a[n]),phi)));}
> >
> >   // prepare for y_b >= SC
> >   for (n in 1:N_b){
> >     eta_b[n] <- exp(dot_product(x_b[n],beta[g_b[n]]));
> >     psi_b[n] <- dot_product(x_b[n],alpha);}
> >
> >   // increment zero alteration
> >   z_a ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_a);
> >   z_b ~ bernoulli_logit(psi_b);
> >
> >   // increment negative binomial model
> >   increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(y_a,eta_a,phi));
> >   increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(y_b,eta_b,phi));
> >
> >   // increment for left hand side truncation of y_b
> >   increment_log_prob(-neg_binomial_2_ccdf_log(SC-1, exp(eta_b),phi));
> > }
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, December 5, 2014 7:45:42 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > > On Dec 4, 2014, at 5:07 PM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Thanks for taking time to look at this Bob,
> > >
> > > (and apologies for my longish reply)
> > >
> > > The derivatives might indeed be the problem. When I run a model without truncation the Gradient evaluation takes 0.06 seconds, and when I run a model with truncation the time taken jumps to 0.45 seconds. These numbers are for a hierarchical regression model with N = 33 000, three groups, and K = 17 predictors.
> > > (with cmdstan--compiled with intel MKL, linux redhat,  2.6 GHz intel processors, 8 or 16GB RAM)
> > >
> > > Given the large N and mostly only weakly correlated predictors, the model should not generally be hard to estimate, I assume.
> > >
> > > The hard constraint on nb_beta (the beta parameter for the negative binomial) is likely not the problem, because the posterior mean is around 0.9.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I have following ideas to speed up the code, maybe you have an opinion about which is most likely to improve speed (the full model is below)?
> > >
> > > (a)
> > > Use more informative priors (i.e. normal(0,1) for betas and chauchy(0,1) for variances.
> > > (I know that nb_beta and all all betas are below 1.) I hope this can address one factor Marc mentioned in his discussion of what influences speed, namely how fast the sampler towards the region of the parameter space with high posteriors
> >
> > This can often help with the number of effective samples per iteration and
> > also improve the iteration times if you find the iterations in the tails
> > take longer (they can if you need more leapfrog steps to get a u-turn).
> >
> > > (b)
> > > Speed up calculations by vectorizing (1) (the second factor Marc mentioned).
> > > In particular, I think of splitting the input by group, i.e. I could submit all relevant variables split by group
> > >
> > > Ngrp1, Ngrp2, Ngrp3, ygrp1, ygrp2, ygrp3, xgrp1, xgrp2, xgrp,
> > >
> > > which would allow to calculate the means as e.g.
> > >
> > > mugrp1 <- beta[1] * xgrp1[1]
> > >
> > > instead of looping through all N and do mu[n] <- beta[g[n]] * x[n]
> >
> > This can help with speed.  Anything that lets you call vector-based
> > log densities with parameters that are mixed vectors and non-vectors
> > will usually let you reuse computations.
> >
> > > (c)
> > > Speed up by vectorizing (2):
> > > Inspired by Marco (Inacio’s) description of a zero-altered NB regression I thought of doing something along these line:
> > > First increment_log_probs gobally as if there were no truncation:
> > >
> > > y ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta)
> > >
> > > Then correct for truncation by incrementing again
> > >
> > > increment_log_prob(na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta))
> > > increment_log_prob(nb*neg_binomial_ccdf_log(SC, alpha,beta))
> > >
> > > whereby SC is the truncation point and na  are the number of people with above the truncation point and nb the number of people below.*
> > >
> > > Somehow I fear that this is a naïve approach, but I think it should be possible to calculate the cdf and ccdf, or actually the entire experession “na*neg_binomial_cdf_log(SC-1, alpha,beta)”, only once. But maybe this is already happening under the hood?
> >
> > This kind of thing can provide a big speedup.  We don't currently reuse
> > the computation because we don't have a vector-based form of the truncated
> > densities, which is what we'd need to do it under the hood.
> >
> > I didn't follow your algebra, but in general, you can do this.  If you
> > N cases of the same density with truncation below at 2, then you just need
> >
> >    increment_log_prob(-N * neg_binomial_ccdf(2, alpha, beta));
> >
> > If the parameters alpha and beta vary by individual, say with a regression,
> > then this won't work.
> >
> > There's a discussion in the manual of what's inserted into the log
> > probability for the various truncations (left/lower, right/upper, both).
> >
> > - Bob
> >

messages.body_plain:
Just in case it hasn't been pointed out: Stan's normal and log-normal distributions use standard deviations (sd), and not precision (1/sd^2). I noticed that you are using (presumed) conjugate gamma priors for precision parameters, which in fact are interpreted as standard deviations in Stan. Although this may not be the cause of the current issues you are running into, it will cause results to differ from an analysis in BUGS/JAGS.

Luc

Now reproduced the same problem with a slightly different model (coralss7mgmt.stan) on another computer. After many iterations, lp__ suddenly becomes -Inf (and so no longer shows on the trace plot). Then n_eff=1 if this happens before the end of the warmup period, and greater than 1 but small if it happens not long after the end). Attached traceplot of lp__: oldchain.pdf. This model contains only normal, multivariate normal and inverse wishart distributions, so the only obvious way this could happen is an overflow. Did it just take a catastrophically bad step? If so, what could I look at to debug it?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: dead-flat traceplots: what's going on?
messages.body_plain:
My guess is that you're using a variable
somewhere that's not defined.  print() is a good way to debug this.
Just print variable values before you use them and you'll usually see
where one snuck by that wasn't initialized.

The other altnernative is tha tyou have some densities that evaluate
to NaN.

Also, the model as written is going to be very inefficient because
you're computing determinants repeatedly rather than computing them
once and re-using the value.  There's also a log_determinant function
that should be more stable than log(determinant(Sigma)), which is prone
to underflow or overflow.

More below on specifics.

> On Dec 17, 2014, at 4:57 PM, Greg Werbin <ourob...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks. I did that, and now I'm getting this error when I try to sample:
>
> Error :
>
> Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
>  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
>
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>
> I attached the second version of my code. I also made some other changes. Am I abusing the ability to declare variables in the model block? Only the regression coefficients are unbounded in the parameters block; surely it can't be the case that there are 100 values between -2 and 2 that are valid for one of the coefs. Or is some kind of initialization happening for other values as well?

Initialization happens for all variables declared as parameters.
We try 100 random initializations of all parameters, and in your
case, none of the 100 random initializations were valid.

This usually means variables not defined or violations of constraints,
though that's usually diagnosed with a warning message.

>
> And I guess here's a feature request: have the warning message state which parameter failed to initialize.

Making this more informative is already pending as a feature request:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/779

But it's not going to be able to isolate a "which parameter failed to initialize"
because initialization doesn't work that way.  There are two potential failure
points,

  1.  while reading in inits from a file or data list/function in R.

      a.  missing value for some parameter

      b.  parameter given value that violates constraint

  2.  while executing log density

Case (1) can be isolated to a given parameter.  Case (2) arises when some
parameters aren't consistent.  For instance, a, b, and c in:

   a ~ uniform(b,c);

This requires a to be initialized between b and c, so there are
multiple ways to fix it by changing subsets of a,b,c.  In some cases,
for some mathmetical functions, we'll get inputs to a non-primitive
function that throws an exception and that we can trap and list.  If
the density just evaluates to -infinity or NaN through primitive
operations (like adding -1/0 as a term), then there's really no way for
us to catch it --- you need to add print statements to figure out when
the log density goes wrong.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I meant you just needed to add

increment_log_prob(0.5 * dot_self(Z[i]));

to the loop to account for the

-0.5 * Z' * (-I) * Z

part of the log copula density. In other words, what you had only did the

-log(R) - 0.5 * Z' * solve(R) * Z

part. You need both parts to obtain

-log(R) - 0.5 * (Z' * (solve(R) - I) * Z)

Ben
