Hi Giorgio

It looks like you put the line:

after adding the listener. However since the call to stan is not blocking, you will get an error because the sampling is not finished. function exitHandler(src,data)
   fprintf('Stan finished. \n');
   mu = src.extract('permuted',true).mu;
   fprintf('mean of mu = %1.2f\n', mean(mu));
end

-b

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
messages.body_plain:
If R-hat is NaN and n_eff is not NaN, it's almost certainly
a precision problemin the arithmetic.

Could you send us a model and data set for which it happens so
we can diagnose?

There may be loss of arithmetic precision in R-hat compared to
what we could do ideally.  The problem is that floating point
subtraction of values close to each other results in so-called
catastrophic cancellation, losing an arbitrary amount of precision.
Something like Welford's algorithm is required to maintain stability
for sample variance calculations, and I'm not sure how PyStan has implemented
R-hat.

For example, this model is problematic arithmetically:

fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(1,1e-20); }")

and produces

          mean  se_mean       sd      2.5%       25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff         Rhat
y            1      0.0        0         1         1   1   1     1  4000          Inf
lp__ -15407440 422002.9 26689805 -61629758 -15407440   0   0     0  4000 1.500106e+14

There's really nothing we can do about such models numerically.  What
you have to do from a user perspective is use a parameterizations

  z = y - 1,

which can be handled stably because you can represent numbers close to zero well.

parameters { real z; } model { z ~ normal(0,1e-20); }

The problem is that there's still no way to represent y = z + 1, but
you can get close to log(y) by using

  log_y <- log1p(z);

We're gradually pulling all these implementations back into
the core Stan C++ code, so at least we'll only have one fix to make
for issues like this in the near future.

- Bob

P.S.  I'm going to drop the above discussion into a new section on
      arithmetic in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
      or maybe an entire chapter on arithmetic stability of various operators.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jesse,

Yes, this is an issue. While R will let you divide by zero (or nearly
zero) quickly and without any problem (other than throwing up an 'Inf'),
Python raises an exception. The current way PyStan handles this probably
isn't the best. If you have a simple case where nan isn't appropriate,
would you mind opening an issue on PyStan's github site?

On the other hand, if there really is zero variance among the chains
with respect to some parameter, rhat and n_eff should be 'nan'.

Thanks,

> > >> we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
> > >> parameters.

> > >> an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
> > >> chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.

> > >> the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter

> > >> code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
messages.body_plain:
Are you using double-precision floating point?  As far as I
know, R's just using standard IEEE floating point.

The usual problems are with subtraction, not division, unless
you get so close to zero that the division overflows to +inf.
But if that happens for two numbers, it should happen in R, too.

And then once you get inf, everything is inf or NaN.  You can't
divide inf/inf or subract (inf - inf), although you can add (inf + inf)
and get inf as long as the infs are the right sign.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Yeah, Python throws an error we have to catch:

> In [4]: 1 / 1e-500
> ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ZeroDivisionError                         Traceback (most recent call last)
> <ipython-input-4-ba7ce1d0dee4> in <module>()
> ----> 1 1 / 1e-500
>
> ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero

rhat and n_eff are bottlenecks on huge models so there's been a lot of
churn trying to get it right AND fast. Originally I had everything going
through Stan and C++ but handing things off to C++ and then handing it
back to Python was too inefficient. If Stan could expose some way for
RStan and PyStan to calculate rhat and n_eff, that would be fantastic.
Right now I believe there are 3 implementations of the rhat and n_eff
calculations (one for each language).

I'd definitely welcome help on this, if anyone is interested.

Thanks,

-a

On 12/18, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Are you using double-precision floating point?  As far as I
> know, R's just using standard IEEE floating point.
>
> The usual problems are with subtraction, not division, unless
> you get so close to zero that the division overflows to +inf.
> But if that happens for two numbers, it should happen in R, too.
>
> And then once you get inf, everything is inf or NaN.  You can't
> divide inf/inf or subract (inf - inf), although you can add (inf + inf)
> and get inf as long as the infs are the right sign.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Dec 18, 2014, at 1:47 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Jesse,
> >
> > Yes, this is an issue. While R will let you divide by zero (or nearly
> > zero) quickly and without any problem (other than throwing up an 'Inf'),
> > Python raises an exception. The current way PyStan handles this probably
> > isn't the best. If you have a simple case where nan isn't appropriate,
> > would you mind opening an issue on PyStan's github site?
> >
> > On the other hand, if there really is zero variance among the chains
> > with respect to some parameter, rhat and n_eff should be 'nan'.
> >
> > Thanks,
> >
> > -a
> >
> >
> > On 12/18, Jesse Bloom wrote:
> >> I sometimes get Rhat values of "nan" when using PyStan. This happens for
> >> certain data sets repeatedly. I think I get these values for variables that
> >> are actually very close to zero and seem well converged based on the
> >> effective sample size (n_eff) values. Is this a bug in stan?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.body_plain:
Reproducible from different initial conditions and seed. Similar behaviour in lp__, step size, and n_divergent.

On Thursday, December 18, 2014 7:02:37 PM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> Plots of lp__, log stepsize, and n_divergent attached. Should it look like that?
>
> The red vertical lines on the bottom two panels are the point where lp__ becomes -Inf. The step size doesn't change at that point. Although n_divergent goes to 1 at that point, there have been lots of 1s before. We get a couple of warning messages:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> cholesky_decompose(N4stan5agrad3varE): mm is not symmetric. m[1,2] is -nan:0, but m[2,1] element is -nan:0
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::inv_wishart_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): LDLT_Factor of random variableunderlying matrix is not positive definite. LDLT_Factor of random variablelast conditional variance is -nan:0.
>
> I was ignoring those, because they only appear at the start.
>
> Will email data and code (and I hope will implement your earlier suggestions for improvements to efficiency when term ends). I'm checking some other initial conditions now.
>
> Thanks
>
> Matt
>
> On Wednesday, December 17, 2014 10:52:20 PM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Does it run into the same problem no matter what the initialization
> > is?
> >
> > What happens to the step sizes at points where it fails and what
> > happens to n_divergent?  The n_divergent variable reports on whether
> > there was an exception or -inf log density that caused the problem.
> >
> > One thing you can try to do is reduce the initial step size and up
> > the target acceptance rate.  That can help you avoid "catastrphically
> > bad steps".
> >
> > We've also relaxed some error checking in some of our multivariate
> > stuff, which may be causing you problems.
> >
> > If you sent us (a) the model in question, (b) the seed you're using
> > to get a bad chain, and (c) the data in a standalone file, we can
> > try running it in the 2.6 release candidate to see if too-strict error checking
> > is the problem.
> >
> > There's also a lot you can do to improve the efficiency of the model as
> > written, but let's get it working first.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Dec 17, 2014, at 3:53 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Now reproduced the same problem with a slightly different model (coralss7mgmt.stan) on another computer. After many iterations, lp__ suddenly becomes -Inf (and so no longer shows on the trace plot). Then n_eff=1 if this happens before the end of the warmup period, and greater than 1 but small if it happens not long after the end). Attached traceplot of lp__: oldchain.pdf. This model contains only normal, multivariate normal and inverse wishart distributions, so the only obvious way this could happen is an overflow. Did it just take a catastrophically bad step? If so, what could I look at to debug it?
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, November 26, 2014 4:46:22 PM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> > > Looks like I spoke too soon. It worked with that particular simulated data set, but with real data, the same problem recurred. There seem to be some other strange things happening on that computer, so it may well be something that isn't directly connected to STAN at all.
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, November 26, 2014 3:30:02 PM UTC, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > > Thanks for checking. I'm glad it's working.
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, November 26, 2014, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Reinstalled, switched to clang++, and it's working again.
> > >
> > > On Saturday, November 22, 2014 4:13:18 PM UTC, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > > Matt,
> > >
> > > Thanks for that info. I'm not really sure how to track this down. Can you try a different compiler or even different optimization level while compiling?
> > >
> > >
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > >
> > > On Sat, Nov 22, 2014 at 11:06 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I think now it must be either a hardware problem or a problem with the installation on that machine. It's reproducible on that machine, but I installed RStan 2.5 on another Ubuntu 12.04 machine, and the same model seemed to run fine.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Friday, November 21, 2014 6:23:33 PM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > That's puzzling.  It's always possible the other machine has
> > > a memory or bus problem in its hardware.  That used to be a lot
> > > more common than it seems to be these days.
> > >
> > > Has anyone reproduced the problem on a different machine, either
> > > Linux or Mac?
> > >
> > > Daniel found another problem with the model seg-faulting/bus-erroring
> > > in diagnostic mode, which is something else we need to fix.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Nov 21, 2014, at 12:42 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Updated code attached (using Bob's suggestion of a normal distribution for initial observations in each time series: didn't fix the problem of n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5 on Ubuntu).
> > > >
> > > > I also installed RStan 2.5 on a machine running 64-bit Windows 7, and this code ran fine (output of sessionInfo() on that computer attached). So either it's a problem that doesn't occur with the Windows version of RStan, or it's just a problem with the installation of RStan 2.5 on one particular Ubuntu machine.
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, November 21, 2014 10:12:30 AM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> > > > Traceplots made using
> > > >
> > > > traceplot(stanres,pars="A")
> > > >
> > > > in RStan
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, November 21, 2014 10:00:43 AM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> > > > Hi Andrew
> > > >
> > > > I think the trace plots are right. I only ran one chain in this case. The four traces are four different parameters (the four elements of a 2 x 2 matrix). The warmup period is only shown on the 2.5 version, but it's the same on the 2.4 version (I saved the 2.4 figure using dev.copy2eps, which doesn't support transparency. My postdoc made the 2.5 version on a different computer, and saved it in some other way).
> > > >
> > > > Matt
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, November 20, 2014 10:31:23 PM UTC, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > > Hi, these traceplots look wrong.  Shouldn’t each chain be a different color on the plot?
> > > >
> > > >> On Nov 20, 2014, at 9:44 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >>
> > > >> Hi Bob
> > > >>
> > > >> Thanks for those suggestions. The only one I've implemented so far is changing the uniform density for y[k] (where firstyear[k]==1 is true) to a normal density (mean 0, standard deviation 10). The uniform density is often used for this kind of model, but a normal with a high standard deviation is also fine. That did sound as though it might be the issue, but turns out it didn't make much difference. The others will take a bit more effort. I'm sure they will make the code more efficient, but I also think that it may be changes to multivariate error checking that are the main reason why we get n_eff=1 for all parameters in STAN 2.5, but not 2.4. I've attached representative trace plots for four of the parameters, under both versions. These have the same pseudorandom number seeds, and it looks like everything is behaving the same for about the first 1800 iterations, and then suddenly the STAN 2.5 version stops changing.
> > > >>
> > > >> Matt
> > > >>
> > > >> On Thursday, November 20, 2014 4:39:25 AM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > >> I don't know much about this kind of model, but we have been
> > > >> tinkering with the multivariate error checking, so that may
> > > >> be causing problems.  But that's probably not the root cause of
> > > >> the problem.
> > > >>
> > > >> For both statistical efficiency (high n_eff per iteration)
> > > >> and computational efficiency (fast iterations), this model
> > > >> needs to be rewritten with Cholesky factor parameters.  The
> > > >> problem is that we can't literally do that for your model because
> > > >> we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
> > > >> parameters.
> > > >>
> > > >> We'd recommend using a correlation matrix parameterization and
> > > >> an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
> > > >> chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.
> > > >>
> > > >> As written, the y[k] where firstyear[k] == 1 will be problematic because
> > > >> the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter
> > > >> declaration for y, which is unconstrained.  This will kill any trajectory
> > > >> explored by the sampler that moves into a region where the density
> > > >> is 0 (outside min_y and max_y).
> > > >>
> > > >> If you really need that uniform density with limited support, you
> > > >> need to declare a different parameter vector with constraint
> > > >> <lower=min_y,upper=max_y> for the parameters y[k] for which
> > > >> firstyear[k] == 1.  But it'll probably be easier just to put
> > > >> a normal density such as
> > > >>
> > > >>   normal((max_y - min_y)/2, (max_y - min_y)/4);
> > > >>
> > > >> For computational efficiency, the best thing to do would be to use
> > > >> the vector form of all the densities.  It'll probably speed up the
> > > >> code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd
> > > >> be a bit tricky with the switch on firstyear[k] == 1 unless you
> > > >> define two local vectors (or even better a separate parameter vectors)
> > > >> for the k such that firstyear[k] == 1;  this is a separate motivation
> > > >> to the constraint).
> > > >>
> > > >> - Bob
> > > >>
> > > >>
> > > >>
> > > >>
> > > >> > On Nov 17, 2014, at 12:54 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >> >
> > > >> > We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is
> > > >> >
> > > >> > y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)
> > > >> >
> > > >> > where mu is a common intercept, a_i is a random intercept, A is a matrix, and Sigma is a covariance matrix. The observation model for the jth observation at the ith site is
> > > >> >
> > > >> > z_j ~ MVN(y_j,Eta)
> > > >> >
> > > >> > where Eta is a covariance matrix. There are some time points at which some sites aren't observed (I've skipped over the details of how we match up observations with corresponding true states).
> > > >> >
> > > >> > In RStan 2.4.0 on 64-bit Ubuntu, everything seemed to work OK (although I'm sure it's not very efficient code). In RStan 2.5.0, if the warmup is long enough, we get n_eff=1 for all parameters (their values remain constant). Maybe we did something wrong that leads to an overflow or underflow, that in turn causes a gradient problem? And somehow we got away with it in 2.4.0?

messages.body_plain:

messages.body_snippet:
Target acceptance increased to 0.99 and initial step size reduced to 1e-5: still essentially the same behaviour. Assuming I'm altering these in the right way:

stanres <- stan(file="../STAN/coralss7mg

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.body_plain:
Matthew,

Try dialing up the acceptance rate to something like 0.999999 and see if the number of n_divergent__ reduces. I had a hierarchical linear model with some nasty geometry that required the adapt_delta higher than 0.99. Also, try leaving the "stepsize" parameter unset, Stan should optimize that in warmup according to the target acceptance rate in adapt_delta.

Rob

On Fri, Dec 19, 2014 at 2:50 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Target acceptance increased to 0.99 and initial step size reduced to 1e-5: still essentially the same behaviour. Assuming I'm altering these in the right way:
>
> stanres <- stan(file="../STAN/coralss7mgmt.stan",data=standata,iter=1e4,chains=1,seed=54321,control=list("adapt_delta",0.99,"stepsize",1e-5))
>
>
> On Friday, December 19, 2014 5:18:31 PM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> > Similar behaviour with target acceptance increased to 0.95. We get many fewer iterations for which n_divergent__ is 1, but we still get lp__ of _Inf after enough iterations (not exactly the same number of iterations as with the default target acceptance).
> >
> > On Friday, December 19, 2014 12:58:36 PM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> > > Reproducible from different initial conditions and seed. Similar behaviour in lp__, step size, and n_divergent.
> > >
> > > On Thursday, December 18, 2014 7:02:37 PM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> > > > Plots of lp__, log stepsize, and n_divergent attached. Should it look like that?
> > > >
> > > > The red vertical lines on the bottom two panels are the point where lp__ becomes -Inf. The step size doesn't change at that point. Although n_divergent goes to 1 at that point, there have been lots of 1s before. We get a couple of warning messages:
> > > >
> > > > Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> > > > cholesky_decompose(N4stan5agrad3varE): mm is not symmetric. m[1,2] is -nan:0, but m[2,1] element is -nan:0
> > > >
> > > > Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> > > > stan::prob::inv_wishart_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): LDLT_Factor of random variableunderlying matrix is not positive definite. LDLT_Factor of random variablelast conditional variance is -nan:0.
> > > >
> > > > I was ignoring those, because they only appear at the start.
> > > >
> > > > Will email data and code (and I hope will implement your earlier suggestions for improvements to efficiency when term ends). I'm checking some other initial conditions now.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks
> > > >
> > > > Matt

> > > > >
> > > > > One thing you can try to do is reduce the initial step size and up
> > > > > the target acceptance rate.  That can help you avoid "catastrphically
> > > > > bad steps".
> > > > >
> > > > > We've also relaxed some error checking in some of our multivariate

> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Allen: Thanks for pointing me to that bug report. The problem does appear to be related to naming of models. A memory explosion occurs if (a) I create a named model and call sampling or (b) I create two models (they don't need to be named) and call sampling on either one. There is no memory explosion with one, unnamed model.

This is enough information for me to work around the problem for now (I think). Should I open a new bug report?

Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
By design, there's no way to convert a real to an integer in Stan.
The problem is that it loses gradient information and we were too
worried people would use it to create models that wouldn't work.

For your application, you can switch to using a while loop.
Instead of:

  for (n in 1:floor(50/0.01))
    ...

which is illegal, you can do:

  {
    int n;
    n <- 1;
    while (n < floor(50/0.01)) {
      ...
      n <- n + 1;
    }
  }

But I wouldn't recommend implementing Euler given that we have a
Runge-Kutta implementation built in.  It's imprecise to autodiff
an iterative algorithm (no error control), and Euler's a lousy
integration algorithm (steps must be too small to maintain error
bounds due to order of error).

- Bob

Some more info: this was a timing test, so I only ran for 200 iterations (100 warmup, 100 sampling). In the warmup phase n_leapfrog as often as high as 2047, and post-warmup it was 1023 on every iteration.

messages.body_plain:
There are two issues:  speed of the implementation code and
speed of the model.

The 1000+ leapfrog steps are the problem because Stan's
evaluating log probs and gradients for each of those steps.
The only way to fix this is to reparameterize or tighten priors.

More warmup iterations might help.  Starting at a lower step
size might also help the warmup go faster.

How is the mixing?  I'd suggest making the treedepth bound even
higher.  I hope it maxing out at different numbers in warmup and
during sampling isn't indicative of an off-by-one error in config
(won't affect sampling accuracy---just how deep the tree can grow
in NUTS).

- Bob

What makes you think there's a problem?  It's OK to get a few
of those messages during warmup.  You can try to crank down the
initial step size lower (say 0.001), which should avoid some of
these messages during warmup.  The problem is that the discretization
of the Hamiltonian needs to find the right step size before
things become arithmetically stable.

data?

messages.body_plain:
The code used to generate coralsim.Rdump isn't likely to be very informative for debugging (all it does is take part of a real data set that I can't distribute, and add some multivariate normal noise to it). Attached anyway so you can see what it was doing (lpdebug5.R).

Probably more useful: a proper simulator that generates data sets with the same structure as a subset of the real data (bivariate time series from each of four coral reefs, each with some missing observations). File coralsim.R, gets the structure of the data set from coralsimexplanatory.Rdata, and uses parameter estimates based on a preliminary run with real data to simulate from a VAR(1) model with Gaussian process error and Gaussian observation error for each reef. Also reproduces the same problem.

It'll certainly be the case that mu (intercept vector), Zeta (covariance matrix for random effect of reef) and b (effect vector for the mgmt explanatory variable, which takes the values 0 or 1) will be very poorly estimated from data sets of this size (four reefs, two with mgmt=1 and two with mgmt=0). Likely to perform much better on the full data set, which contains many more reefs, but runs much more slowly. In any case, poorly identified parameters shouldn't (I think) lead to a proposal with lp_ = -Inf being accepted?

Matt

and where the arguments are declared --- you can only transform
data variables in the transformed data block.

Some of our distributions, like Poisson, directly accept log-scale
arguments so you don't need to exponentiate at all.

To help more, we'd need to see the model.

Hi Joshua,

Hopefully you saw the comment on the github issue. We intentionally did not include forward mode autodiff in Stan's general model header: src/stan/model/model_header.hpp.

For the time being, you should include headers before including the model header:
#include <stan/agrad/fvar.hpp>
#include <stan/agrad/fvar/matrix.hpp>

Including those before including the model header will bring in the forward mode template specializations that are needed for your program.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 29, 2014, at 6:32 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> In section 16.3 on functions accessing the log_prob accumulator, there's this example which the document says:
>
>
> Here is an example of a function to return the centered coefficients derived from a
> non-centered vector of parameters beta_raw along with the location mu of the center
> and the scale sigma; see Section 19.1 for more information on centering.
>
> Here's the example:
>
> functions {
>   vector center_lp(vector beta_raw, real mu, real sigma) {
>     beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
>     sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
>     mu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>     return sigma * beta_raw + mu;
>   }
> }
>
>
> To me it looks like the first thing that happens is a call to:
>
> normal_log(beta_raw,0,1)
>
> So I'm confused but here's my interpretation:  after sampling beta_raw will look like it has a distribution N(0,1)... which means the function
> is in fact using a centered parameterization of (random) effects along with a mean and standard deviation to produce a vector of non-centered
> coefficients for use in regression.
>
> Am I right about this?

No.  The terminology in the literature is confusing.
The beta_raw has a NON-centered parameterization and the
return value of the function will be centered around mu (at
least if nothing else is going on in the model).

It's what we used to call the "Matt trick" because Matt Hoffman independently
suggested it before we realized there was a literature on it.

>  If so, could the documentation be re-written to emphasize the effect of using such a function? Something along
> the lines of
>
> Here is an example of a function to assign standard normal priors to a vector of coefficients, along with a center and scale, and return the
> translated and scaled coefficients.  It can be used to generate transformed parameters while maintaining a centered parameterization.

I think your formulation is clearer.  And it needs a cross-ref to
the section of the manual talking about centered and non-centered
parameterizations!

> What I'm really trying to do is sort out the meaning of this code: becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/diabcvd/wei_lap_joint.stan <http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/diabcvd/wei_lap_joint.stan>

so can probably help out.

Sorry about that.

Hi,

I'm learning to use stan (rather slowly) and I've found something odd.

Specifically, a linear regression, using the radon data, of log(radon) ~ log(uranium) gives radically different results when fitted with lm() and when fitted with rStan. The intercept is much too low, and the effect estimate is a little higher than the lm() estimate. By contrast, the linear regression of log(radon) against floor, gives almost exactly the same results each way.

The reason is, I think, because the draws for the intercept and the effect of uranium are highly negatively correlated (see the second pairs plot). This is turn relates, but I don't quite see how, to the fact that the uranium level is a property of the county (one of 85) where the house (one of 919) in which the measurement was done is located.

I attach a pdf with the details. Any thoughts (other than do graphs and simple analyses first!)?

Regards,
Anthony Staines

If you have a constant c and write:

  (y - c) ~ logormal(log_mu, sigma);

Then y has a shifted lognormal.  It's a linear transform,
so there's no Jacobian adjustment necessary (ignore any warning
messages that might pop up).

> On Dec 31, 2014, at 4:45 PM, Andrew Ellis <a.w....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> wow, that was fast. Thanks very much...
>
> But what if I need to estimate the shift parameter c, i.e.  c ~ uniform(0, min(y))?

If y and c are both parameters, the transform is just

  (y, c) -> (y-c, c)

which gives you a lower triangular Jacobian with
a determinant of 1,

  d(y-c)/dy   dc/dy          1   0
                       =
  d(y-c)/dc   dc/dc         -1   1

Just make sure to declare c with the relevant constraints

parameters {
  ...
  real<lower=0, upper=min(y)> c;

If only c is a parameter, then the map is just

  c -> (y-c)

and d(y-c)/dc = -1, so the absolute value's 1 and you're good to go
with no Jacobian adjustment.

- Bob

CmdStan.  I'm working on a reproducible case but having trouble reducing
run-time below a day...

I guess that it's possible that this results from some inter-process
issue.  The Stan executables are invoked from make which is invoked by a
controlling Java application which generates the model and/or data files
involved.  Further, this occurred in the context of running that Java
application with the Eclipse IDE (with debugging).  It also will not
surprise me if this a Windows-specific issue, whether with regard to
inter-process and/or buffered IO limitations that are less prevalent in
other operating systems (imo).

If I succeed in reproducing it in that environment I will then try it
from the command line directly and advise if there is a problem, perhaps
after trying it under Linux first.  This will take a few days to complete.

Good to know such a thing is unprecedented.

Thanks,
Paul

One thing you could do is try using Stan's optimize to see if it
finds the same mode.  The posterior mean isn't guaranteed to be near
the posterior mode (though I'd expect them to be reasonably close for
a regression like this).  Maybe someone else will have an idea about
what's going on.

For your model, you want to declare the sd parameter as

  real<lower=0> sigma;

The constraint in the declaration should match the support in the model.

Your Stan models didn't render in that knitr.  Here's what I did in knitr
to render Stan programs:

```{r comment=NA}
file_path <- "soil_incubation.stan";
lines <- readLines(file_path, encoding="ASCII");
for (n in 1:length(lines)) cat(lines[n],'\n');
```

I couldn't find any built-in way to include a file in knitr,
but I'd love to hear better suggestions than the above hack.

- Bob
